title: Diet analysis of coyotes at the edge of their expanding range in Long Island, NY
content:
Abstract
Coyotes (Canis latrans) have only recently spread from mainland New York State into the large and highly urbanized islands of New York Harbor, including the over 3500 km2 Long Island. Here, we present the first data collected on the diets of some of the first coyotes to colonize central and eastern Long Island. Vegetation, northern raccoons (Procyon lotor) and cottontail rabbits (Sylvilagus sp.) were the most common food items overall; though prey assemblages did vary by site coyotes consumed an array of small mammals everywhere. No domestic cats and dogs were found in our samples. Anthropogenic items were limited (paper, plastic, etc. was present in <10% of all scats and < 4% of all food items) as well. White-tailed deer (Odocoileus virginianus), domestic cats (Felis cattus), and birds appeared less frequently in Long Island scat than in NYC, while raccoons and cottontails appeared more frequently. In the future greater effort should be made to identify avian remains more precisely because bird remains were present in over 20% of scats from some of our sites. This information is a valuable first step in exploring potential trophic effects of coyotes in this new area, providing information on coyote ecology to a local community, and fostering better human-wildlife coexistence as millions of Long Island residents become aware of their new neighbors.
